network_thesis.headline: The by-the-seat air brand meets the water surface it already stands on.
network_thesis.body: Blade built the premium by-the-seat mobility brand of the New York waterfront: scheduled helicopter and seaplane seats from Manhattan's own docks and heliports to JFK, Newark and the Hamptons, sold through its own booking flow. Since August 2025 that Passenger business belongs to Joby Aviation, which is carrying the same customer base toward electric vertical flight as certification arrives. Blade's customers already stand on the region's piers and heliports every week. Navier adds a water tier under that same brand and habit — a foiling electric boat, booked the same way, at a lower seat price than the helicopter, and running in weather that grounds rotorcraft.

network_thesis.how_to_read: Each corridor below runs from a dock or heliport Blade customers already use. LaGuardia is new inventory — Blade has no scheduled by-the-seat air product on that run today. The two Hamptons legs sit directly alongside Blade's own $795 helicopter seat, at a lower Navier price.
network_thesis.coverage_note: The same fleet proving these four corridors extends across the wider harbor and Long Island Sound as further corridors are mapped, with no new terminals needed beyond the docks and heliports Blade already operates from.

partner_context.their_ambition: You built the premium by-the-seat air mobility brand of the New York region — scheduled helicopter and seaplane seats from Manhattan to JFK, Newark and the Hamptons, sold and ticketed through your own app. Since August 2025 you're part of Joby Aviation, carrying that customer base toward electric vertical flight as certification arrives.
partner_context.their_pressure: Helicopters are loud, weather-grounded and capacity-constrained: a five-minute JFK hop or a Hamptons weekend seat is a premium product with a ceiling on both price and volume. The surface between your air routes — the harbor and the Sound itself — is served by neither your aircraft nor anyone else's booked, by-the-seat product.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier adds a water tier under the same premium, by-the-seat model you already run: foiling electric boats, booked the same way, departing the same docks and heliports — including East 34th Street, where Blade already operates a lounge — at a lower seat price than the helicopter, with weather resilience the helicopter doesn't have.

hero.title: BLADE × Navier — the water tier under the air brand
hero.subtitle: Blade sells the premium seat from Manhattan's docks and heliports. Navier fills in the surface underneath.
hero.what_we_do_together: We add a foiling, all-electric water tier to Blade's by-the-seat network — the same booking flow, the same premium positioning, departing East 34th Street and other Blade nodes. Navier brings the vessels and the water operating model; Blade brings the demand, the brand, and the terminal footprint already built across the harbor and the Hamptons.

why_now: Blade's helicopter product tops out at the price and weather ceiling of rotorcraft: fog and high wind ground the fleet, and every seat costs what it costs to fly a helicopter. Foiling water craft lift clear of the chop, run in conditions that ground helicopters, and undercut both the $795 Hamptons seat and the $195 JFK seat on price — while opening routes, like LaGuardia, that Blade doesn't fly today.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel is fast, smooth and quiet rather than pounding through chop — and it runs in sea states that keep helicopters grounded. It's electric on the harbor legs and hybrid on the longer Hamptons runs, so the seat cost structure looks nothing like a helicopter's.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier operates from the docks and heliports Blade's customers already use — East 34th Street chief among them — needing only a berth pedestal, not a new terminal or heliport.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Blade's passenger business just joined Joby, a company built around the next generation of vertical flight and already thinking about what comes after the helicopter. A proven, lower-cost, weather-resilient water tier is a natural complement to that transition, not a competitor to it.

multimodal_fit: Blade already runs premium, ticketed, by-the-seat mobility with its own booking flow and terminal network. A Navier water tier slots into the same footprint: the East 34th Street node serves both today, and a rider could book a harbor hop or a Hamptons water leg the same way they book a helicopter seat.

differentiation.why_navier: Weather resilience Blade's rotorcraft can't match — boats operate in wind and fog that grounds helicopters. A materially lower seat price on every mapped corridor, including the marquee Hamptons run. And far higher seat volume per vessel over a season, without the noise and community pushback that constrain helicopter frequency.

proof_points.claim: Blade's passenger business is now part of Joby Aviation.
proof_points.evidence: Joby Aviation acquired Blade's Passenger business in August 2025; the former public parent, Blade Air Mobility, Inc. (NASDAQ: BLDE), sold the Passenger business and rebranded as Strata Critical Medical, Inc. (NASDAQ: SRTA).
proof_points.source: Joby transaction announcement, 2025-08-04; Strata Q1 2026 results

proof_points.claim: Blade runs an asset-light, by-the-seat model.
proof_points.evidence: Blade does not own or operate aircraft; all flights are operated by DOT/FAA-licensed direct carriers, and Blade sells scheduled seats, shared charter and private charter through its own booking platform and terminal/lounge network.

proof_points.claim: The Passenger business generates real, growing seat revenue.
proof_points.evidence: FY2024 Passenger revenue was $101.876M; in the last reported quarter before the sale (Q2 2025), Short Distance revenue was $17.195M on 22,730 passenger seats flown.

proof_points.claim: Blade's current Northeast pricing sets the bar Navier beats.
proof_points.evidence: JFK seats start at $195; Hamptons seats start at $795, with 2026 destinations including Sag Harbor, East Hampton and Montauk.
proof_points.source: BLADE JFK page; BLADE Hamptons page, accessed 2026-07-28

proof_points.claim: Blade already operates from the same waterfront node Navier does.
proof_points.evidence: Blade's East 34th Street lounge (Lounge East) serves EWR and weekday JFK flights — the same East River node as Navier's East 34th Street boarding point.
proof_points.source: BLADE JFK page; BLADE brand facts

objections.concern: Winter weather and seasonality could limit water service.
objections.response: Harbor commuter corridors (LGA, Paulus Hook) run year-round; the Hamptons legs are seasonal by nature — Blade's own Hamptons product only runs May through September, so a matching Navier season is the market norm, not a shortfall.

objections.concern: A cheaper water seat could cannibalize Blade's own helicopter revenue.
objections.response: The two products serve different jobs: the helicopter is the five-minute flight; the boat is the everyday workhorse at a fraction of the airport fare and below the Hamptons ticket. Blade's own Hamptons passes already blend helicopter and seaplane seats — a water tier is one more mode in the same by-the-seat menu, aimed at riders who'd otherwise book a car or a train, not just splitting existing helicopter demand.

objections.concern: Above six passengers, US operators need Coast Guard certification.
objections.response: Pioneer II (N30, 8-passenger) is built for exactly this path: operating above six passengers requires USCG Subchapter T small-passenger-vessel certification, a known, navigable certification route rather than an open regulatory question — the fleet plan for these corridors is scoped to it from day one.

objections.concern: Dock access at Blade's own nodes isn't guaranteed.
objections.response: Blade's East 34th Street lounge already sits on the waterfront it uses for ground transport to its flights; the ask here is co-location for a Navier berth pedestal alongside existing terminal infrastructure, not a new site.

the_ask.navier_brings: The foiling fleet — Pioneer II for the harbor corridors, Quanta-LR hybrid for the Hamptons legs — captain operations, and the USCG certification path for passenger vessel service.
the_ask.partner_brings: The demand, the by-the-seat brand and booking flow, and terminal access starting at East 34th Street.
the_ask.next_step: Pilot the East 34th Street–LaGuardia and Pier 11–Paulus Hook harbor corridors first to prove the daily-commute case, then extend into the Hamptons legs for the following season.

close.title: The water tier under the air brand.
close.body: Blade sells the premium seat above the harbor. Navier fills in the surface underneath — same docks, same by-the-seat model, at a lower price and in weather the helicopter can't fly.

ladder_transitions.headline: Same 10% capture, expanded to the full mapped network
ladder_transitions.basis: Width-only step. Capture rate held at 10%; corridor set expands from sourced flagships to the full mapped network.

ladder_transitions.headline: Network matures: faster, more comfortable boats grow the market + leading-operator capture
ladder_transitions.basis: Two-lever step. (1) Faster, more comfortable boats grow the cross-water market (induced demand). (2) Leading-operator capture lifts share from 10% floor to 25% mature, network-wide.

ladder_transitions.headline: Lens shift: Navier captured share → total inducible marine-transfer wallet
ladder_transitions.basis: Unit change. Divide SAM (the captured share) by leading-operator capture rate to recover the full inducible water-transfer market — the marine-mobility TAM.

ladder_transitions.headline: Marine transfer → total journey wallet (food, stays, experiences, in-app ads)
ladder_transitions.basis: Journey-wallet step. Each $1 of marine-transfer spend unlocks ~$3 of broader journey GMV across merchants the partner monetizes.
